ai.title: SDK trust gate extends to MCP servers and registry id validation
ai.summary: The trust gate now treats MCP servers listed by a remote agent template as executable content, refusing unpublished publisher templates that define them unless the publisher is trusted. `fetchAgentFromDatabase` validates the publisher, agent, and version segments against `PUBLISHED_ID_SEGMENT` and `PUBLISHED_VERSION` before building the registry URL, blocking ids that could rewrite the path. The `UntrustedAgentPublisherError` message and `hasExecutableContent` helper are exported for callers and tests.
ai.evidence: The diff adds `hasExecutableContent` to `sdk/src/agent-publisher-trust.ts`, which treats both executable `handleSteps` source strings and the presence of MCP servers as executable content, and switches `checkRemoteAgentTemplateTrust` to call it instead of `hasExecutableHandleSteps`. `sdk/src/impl/database.ts` adds the `PUBLISHED_ID_SEGMENT` and `PUBLISHED_VERSION` regex constants and an early guard in `fetchAgentFromDatabase` that rejects IDs violating them before URL construction. New tests in `sdk/src/impl/__tests__/fetch-agent-publisher-trust.test.ts` assert that untrusted publishers with MCP servers are refused and that registry-path-rewriting IDs are refused before any fetch.
ai.unknowns: The diff does not show a consumer wiring `hasExecutableContent` outside the trust module, and it is unclear whether any previously-accepted untrusted MCP-enabled template is expected to keep loading after this change.

eli5.text: The trust check for downloadable agents now also covers agents that connect to external tools (MCP servers): a remote agent from a publisher you haven't approved will be refused if it lists external tools or executable program code, not just if it includes custom code. The agent address is also checked before the request is sent, so a crafted publisher, agent, or version name can no longer redirect the lookup to a different agent on the registry. This closes a gap where pulling anyone's public agent could silently spawn external processes or connect to outside tools on your machine. Internal tooling change with no direct effect on end users unless they run ad-hoc remote agents, in which case untrusted ones that reach out to external servers or code will now be blocked by default.

ai.title: Freebucks timezone header now filters remote-host and invalid zones
ai.summary: The timezone header reported for Freebucks billing-timezone checks is no longer the raw Intl-resolved zone. It now passes through freebucksDeviceTimeZone, which drops zones the runtime cannot tell ('Etc/Unknown' and blanks), fixed-offset Windows zones parsed with DST off, and UTC that comes from a remote host (SSH, Codespaces, Gitpod, REMOTE_CONTAINERS, GITPOD_WORKSPACE_ID) or an unparseable TZ, so a dev container or SSH box no longer reports the image's UTC as the user's home day. freebucksTimeZoneHeaders now takes an optional FreebucksTimeZoneRuntime so callers and tests can inject the zone, platform and env instead of always reading the live process. The new tests assert each of those filtering cases and that a local machine genuinely set to UTC still reports UTC.

New exports: FreebucksTimeZoneRuntime, freebucksDeviceTimeZone; new env reads: REMOTE_CONTAINERS, GITPOD_WORKSPACE_ID; new constant ETC_OFFSET_ZONE = /^Etc\/GMT[+-]\d{1,2}$/.

testNames: a crashed writer no longer prevents deleting a saved connection
recovery preserves a live owner even when its lock is old
competing processes recover a legacy PID lock without losing writes
throwing from an operation releases its lock for the next writer

facts: Publish an already-complete PID atomically. Creating an empty lock and then writing its owner leaves an unrecoverable lock if killed between.
EPERM (including another user's process) is not evidence of death.
Recover PID locks without allowing two reapers to unlink a successor's lock.

A second filesystem lock would itself survive a crash. A loopback listener is a short-lived, kernel-released reaper mutex on every supported OS. Key it by the observed PID, so aliases of the configuration path share the mutex. Collisions only defer recovery; they never allow concurrent reapers.
Re-read under the mutex: another reaper may already have removed the old lock and a writer may now own the pathname. Never expire a live PID by age.
entries.title: SDK update: byok

ai.title: SDK recovers stale BYOK connection lock via PID check
ai.summary: `createBunByokMetadataStore`'s `withLock` now publishes the owning PID to an atomic lock candidate and uses `fs.link` to claim `connections.lock`, so a process killed between creating the lock file and writing its PID no longer leaves an unrecoverable lock. `sdk/src/impl/byok-lock.ts` adds `recoverByokLock`, which calls `recoverByokLock(lock)` on `EEXIST`: it reads the lock's owner, treats `EPERM` (including another user's process) as not dead, uses a loopback listener on port `49152 + (Number(owner) % 16384)` as a short-lived kernel-released reaper mutex keyed by the observed PID, and re-reads the owner under that mutex before unlinking the lock so it never expires a live PID by age or removes a successor's lock. Tests cover a crashed writer not blocking connection deletion, recovery preserving a live owner even when its lock is old, competing reapers not losing writes, and an operation that throws releasing its lock.
ai.evidence: New file `sdk/src/impl/byok-lock.ts` exports `recoverByokLock`; `sdk/src/byok.ts` imports it and calls `await recoverByokLock(lock)` from within the `withLock` method of `createBunByokMetadataStore` when `fs.link(candidate, lock)` throws `EEXIST`. The `withLock` implementation now writes `String(process.pid)` to a per-call `connections-lock-<uuid>.tmp` candidate with { flag: 'wx', mode: 0o600 } and hard-links that candidate to `connections.lock` via `fs.link(candidate, lock)`, replacing the prior `fs.open(lock, 'nx')` + `handle.writeFile` approach.
ai.unknowns: Whether the new lock scheme changes the on-disk lock path shape or how the Desktop settings UI surfaces the updated retry message.

ai.title: Uuidv7 generator for append-heavy primary keys
ai.summary: Adds `uuidv7` in `common/src/util/uuidv7.ts`, producing RFC 9562 version-7 UUIDs whose first 48 bits hold a Unix-millisecond timestamp, version 7 and variant 10xx bits enforced over the random bytes, returned as a standard hyphenated UUID string. The JSDoc explains it targets append-heavy primary keys such as `agent_run` (COD-751), where v4's random placement dirties random btree pages and re-writes whole WAL pages after checkpoints, whereas v7's time ordering appends to rightmost pages. Tests assert well-formedness, timestamp encoding in the high 48 bits, version/variant bit stability under zero and all-ones random sources, monotonic string sorting across consecutive milliseconds, uniqueness of 10000 ids minted in the same millisecond, and compatibility with the zod `.uuid()` and `z.uuid()` validators the run and step schemas use.
ai.evidence: New file `common/src/util/uuidv7.ts` exports `uuidv7(now = Date.now(), random = crypto.getRandomValues)`, encoding a 48-bit Unix-millisecond timestamp in the first 48 bits, setting version 7 and variant 10xx bits, with accompanying tests in `common/src/util/__tests__/uuidv7.test.ts`; the JSDoc references (`agent_run`, COD-751) ties the motivation to append-heavy primary keys.
